analytic.title: An Application using Pinwheel Scheduling Model

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Real-time systems, ranging from small portable devices or embedded systems to more complex generalpurpose computers, are designed to satisfy various of real-time computation. It is the most important to guarantee all the requests will be satisfied correctly in time. Rate monotonic algorithm is the most wellknown real-time scheduling algorithm in the periodic task model. It not only has high schedulability, but also has a tight utilization bound to easily check whether the task set is feasible. In rate monotonic algorithm, a task will be executed once in each period, but the start time of execution might be different in each period. On the contrary, for tasks scheduled using pinwheel model, the execution schedule in each period will be always the same. Therefore, pinwheel scheduling model is very suitable for real-time systems which need high predictability. The pinwheel scheduling model transforms the task periods into harmonic numbers shorter than or equal to the original periods and provides many advantageous scheduling features. However, not all tasks allow to do the transformation and some would like to be executed according to their original periods. In this paper, we discuss how to solve the problem and give an application in power-aware real-time scheduling, where we can see the pinwheel model is very important in current embedded system design with power-aware requirement.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Recently, applications of embedded systems increase rapidly, especially on mobile devices and portable systems. These mobile embedded systems are mostly made with multiple fancy functions and thus real-time constraints are usually required. For example, if a personal digital assistant does not have a real-time response when doing GPS (Global Positioning System) routing, we might feel that it is clumsy or malfunctioned. However, building a reliable real-time embedded system which can guarantee the tasks from missing deadlines or can have graceful degradation when missing deadline needs combination of advanced hardware and software technologies. Excluding the hardware design techniques and performance issues, real-time operating system is the most critical part to the success of these embedded systems. A good real-time operating system would have the upper bound of any latency in the kernel, and an efficient scheduler to guarantee that all the tasks will meet their timing constraints without too much overhead. The integration of welldesigned real-time operating system and high performance hardware will be the base of a high performance real-time embedded system. As we know the kernel of a RTOS is scheduling, therefore, a good scheduling is a primal requirement to obtain good perform in a realtime system. We discuss two real-time scheduling using priority-driven approach and time-driven approach respectively.

div.head: Rate Monotonic Algorithm
div.p: In real-time systems, there are many ways to model a system, such as periodic task model [12], distanceconstrained task model [11], aperiodic task model [2], etc. Since there are many periodical activities in our daily life, many previous works were based on the periodic task model. In the periodic task model, each task T i has a (worst case) execution time e i , period P i and infinite jobs J i,j where j, ≥ 1, is the counter for number of jobs. Every job will be executed exactly once in each period, and the execution of the jobs is independent. To be simple, it is usually assumed that every task is ready at time 0 and the deadline of each job is at the end of each period. That is, each job J i,j has its own deadline at j • P i .
In priority-driven scheduling, the scheduler always schedule the task with the highest priority to be ex-time J i,j J i,j+1 J i,j+2

Rate monotonic scheduling (RMS) algorithm [12] is a priority-driven scheduling algorithm using the periodic task model, where a task with shorter period has higher priority. It is the optimal fixed priority scheduling algorithm in terms that if any other fixed priority scheduling can find a feasible schedule, RMS can find one, too.

There have been many papers working on related issues, but most of them focus on reducing the complexity of schedulablility test [1], [13]. However, when scheduling a real-time task set, RMS algorithm can not provide a reasonable distance constraint. In other words, suppose the distance between two successive jobs, J i,j and J i,j+1 , is the difference of the finish times of two consecutive jobs. The distance is greater than e i and less than 2P i -e i , shown in Figure 1. We can see that the distance is indeterministic, and therefore degrades predictability of real-time systems.

In real world, applications need distance constraint. Changing engine oil of a vehicle would be a good example. Suppose the engine oil needs to be changed every six months to keep the engine working well. If we take this job as a periodic task and use rate monotonic algorithm to schedule, we will find that the first oil changing may be done on January and the second may be done on December. This result is not good for any vehicle, because the distance between two oil changings could be up to eleven months. Pinwheel model can be used to solve this problem.

div.head: Pinwheel Algorithm and DCTS
div.p: In some real-time applications, tasks must be executed in a distance-constrained manner, rather than just periodically [5]. There is another class of realtime systems called Distance-Constrained Task System (DCTS). In a DCTS task set T= {T 1 , T 2 , • • • , T n }, every task T i consists of infinite sequence of jobs J i,1 , J i,2 , J i,3 ,• • • , and job J i,j+1 must be started only after J i,j has finished executing. Task T i has execution time e i and distance constraint c i . The distance between two consecutive jobs of a task is defined to be the difference of the finish times of these two jobs. Let f i,j denote the finish time of job J i,j , for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and j ≥ 1. The distance between J i,j and J i,j+1 is defined to be f i,j+1f i,j . The distance constraint requires that f i,j+1f i,j ≤ c i , for all j ≥ 1. Besides, the jobs are preemptable.

Based on the privious work [6], pinwheel algorithm is applied to solve scheduling problem on DCTS. The pinwheel problem is defined as follows [7]. Given a multiset of n positive integers A = {a 1 , a 2 , • • • , a n }, the pinwheel problem is to find an infinite sequence over the symbols {1, 2, • • • , n} such that there is at least one symbol i within any subsequence of a i consecutive symbols. Thus, using pinwheel model to schedule DCTS would be a good solution. It can guarantee the distance constraints of real-time systems.

Transforming real-time task sets using pinwheel model , for which we call pinwheel transformation in the latter of the paper, has several advantages. First, because of the harmonic periods after transformation, the scheduled jobs have regular behavior with distanceconstraint and the hyperperiod can be easily derived. Second, because of the harmonic periods and known start times and finish times, the next idle time can easily be predicted. Third, the schedule of tasks and the predictable idle time could help system to adjust the voltage or frequency level to reduce power consumption.

Pinwheel model seems to have many advantages to real-time systems, but the point is that once the tasks are transformed to harmonic periods, all these new periods will be equal to or shorter than the original periods. Therefore, the execution of a task may become frequently. Take changing engine oil for example again. When using pinwheel model, although it is guaranteed that oil would be changed in a fixed period (distance constraint) , however, it may be changed too frequently, for example once every five months.

In this paper, we would like to make pinwheel model more applicable in real-time systems, and prove that tasks transformed by pinwheel algorithm can still have some characteristics of original period. That is the execution of some real-time tasks using the original period after pinwheel transformation. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the problem and proves that pinwheel algorithm is able to maintain the distance constraint and the same execution time in original periods. Section 3 is an example of applying pinwheel model to a power-aware real-time system. And this paper is concluded in Section 4.

div.head: Retain Original Period in Pinwheel Model
div.p: For example, suppose a system has five tasks with distance constraints {9.2, 10.6, 10.7, 21.4, 23.4}, respectively, and their execution times are {1.5, 2.0, 3.4, In some real-time such as video player, are a kind of real-time application with distanceconstraint. In order to play a video clip smoothly, it requires to decode 30 frames per second. In other words, we can take this application as a periodic task with distance constraint, and the task has its period of 33 ms. The decoder has to generate a frame within 33 ms. If this requirement is satisfied, we will see a smooth video clip replay. At least, a real-time system should guarantee us something like the example above. In a high workload real-time system, if the jobs are executed without distance constraints, the video clip may be delayed randomly. In Figure 1, we can clearly see that the longest distance between two consecutive jobs of a periodic task is up to 2P ie i . In this scenario, suppose the execution time of video decoding is 10 ms. The longest distance is up to 56 ms, which is about 70% of the period. Lemma 1 is obvious resulting from the harmonic periods after pinwheel transformed. However, pinwheel transformation has a side effect. With scheduling of the period, the job execution frequency of a periodic task is increasing. Therefore, if a video decoder with period of 33 ms is transformed by pinwheel algorithm, it may generate more than 30 frames per second. Although all of the jobs are not missing their deadline, the video clip will look like fast-forwarding. Although pinwheel algorithm provides more benefits to a realtime system, the problem of changing task's period is still critical. In fact, pinwheel model can keep the job execution frequency and eliminate the problem of the side effect. In Figure 3, take T 1 for example, after pinwheel transformation, the period of T 1 is 5.3, and the original period of T 1 is 9.2, which is represented by a dotted line. Figure 2(a) shows that the original execution time of T 1 is 1.5. Although, in Figure 2(b), the execution time is still unchanged in every period, the new period is shorter. Consequently, in Figure 3, it is obvious to see that the schedule delimited by original period contains extra execution time. By observation, if we make the extra execution times of new schedule become idle times, the problem can be eliminated.

div.head: Theorem 1 For a given task set, after pinwheel transformation, the execution time of a task within any original period is larger than or equal to the original execution time.
div.p: Proof 1 When the original periods are transformed to harmonic periods, the new periods are shorter than or equal to the original periods and the jobs are executed exactly using the same execution time from the beginning of each new periods. According to Lemma 1, Figure 4 show that with the same distance between any two of the successive jobs, if we use new period as a window to delimit any time slice, no matter where the

And we know that new period is shorter than or equal to the original period. Therefore, if we take original period as a window to delimit time slice, we will get a longer time slice than original execution time. According to the previous inferences, we can say that the execution time of new schedule delimited by original period must be equal to or longer than the execution time delimited by new periods.

Because jobs of a task in a pinwheel schedule was the same distance, the deadline or start time of two consecutive jobs will all equal to the distance. According to the inference, suppose there is a task transformed by pinwheel algorithm, and there is a window composed of T and T . In Figure 4, let T -T = P , where P is the period of the task, and let T become the start time of a period. Then, we can see that the execution time in T -T equals to the execution time in P . Furthermore, if we shift the window by adding a real number d, because of the distance-constraint, we will realize that the execution time will still be the same. Based on the result, if we let T -T ≥P , the result is that the execution time in T -T will be longer than or equal to the original execution time. Thus, the new execution time delimited by time slice T -T is larger than or equal to the original execution time.

This inference telling that pinwheel model based real-time system is capable to maintain the original job execution frequency. In the video clip example, at last, the job execution frequency after pinwheel transformation is increased and makes the video looks like fastforwarding. Now, we all realize that even the execution time is extended in original periods, we can claim that the new schedule contains enough execution time to finish the jobs in original periods. Therefore, if we can eliminate the extra execution times, we can retain the job execution frequency in pinwheel schedule. Actually, the answer is simple. After calculation, we can treat the extra execution time as idle time. Once the extra execution time is treated as idle time, the execution frequency will equal to the original frequency, and this real-time system is still feasible without affecting other tasks, which might have distance constrains.

As shown in Figure 6, after compacting the schedule, there exists some new slacks in the pinwheel schedule. By determining the idle time in a pinwheel schedule, it will be great help in many aspect. For example, the idle time can be reversed for aperiodic tasks or using for dynamic frequency scaling in power-aware scheduling. In the next section, we discussed the application on power-aware real-time systems.

div.head: Application
div.p: Recently, in the 3C industry, many hand-held devices are made as small as possible. According to the development of hand-held devices, multimedia would be the main application of these devices. As we know, multimedia applications need more processing power, such as high performance codec, to complete the tasks.

However, high performance brings high power consumption. With the requirement of small size for these devices, battery size is also limited. Moreover, long lifetime is also required for these devices. Therefore, power-aware becomes a critical issue on hand-held devices. Power-aware means that the system is aware of how to make the most use of electricity power to complete the tasks. It is not only trying to make the system using as low power as possible and it will sometimes consume more power to get the task done as soon as possible. For example, even though we can impose more cost and use lithium battery to extend the lifetime of hand-held devices, using power-aware operating system is the most effective and economical way to extend the lifetime of hand-held devices. Based on the power consumption equation from previous research [16], [3], the power consumption is calculated as following:
div.formula: P = N sw • C • 2 dd • f,
div.p: where P is the power consumption, N sw is the switched gate count on the integrated circuit, C is the capacitance of the integrated circuit, V 2 dd is the input voltage and f represents the frequency of the integrated circuit. If we want to reduce the power consumption, the parameters above would be the basics. The N sw is related to the design of opcode and instruction set, the C is changed when the manufacturing process is different and most popular research issue is on the parameter V 2 dd and f . Therefore, the common used techniques in reducing the power consumption are Dynamic Voltage scaling (DVS) and Dynamic Frequency Scaling (DFS). DFS and DVS allow the changing of processor frequency and supply voltage. Scheduling using DFS and DVS is to determine the frequency along with the voltage of a processor [17,4] whenever a job is executing. DFS and DVS can be implemented in various levels of a system, such as in the processor, in the OS scheduler, in the compiler, or in the application [14]. If it is difficult to reduce the switched gate count, lower the voltage or frequency of processors while still meet performance requirement would be a good alternative. And, with the growth of battery technology and poweraware design, the lifetime of hand-held devices could be long enough to support multimedia applications.

In the past few years, DVS and DFS are the most popular and efficient techniques to reduce power consumption [8], [18]. However, the complexity will be too high if we would like to have a more systematic or analytic result instead of just heuristics to reduce power consumption. Taking advantages of pinwheel scheduling model, the schedule is regular and can be derived in polynomial time. Therefore, it is possible to optimize using DVS and DFS in a more efficient way [15]. In Figure 7, it shows the idea of decreasing the processing frequency to reduce the power consumption. Tasks T 1 , T 3 , and T 4 are rescheduled using different frequencies and result in longer execution times. To decrease the voltage or frequency, there should be enough idle time followed to adjust possible longer execution time. If we can know efficiently where will be the idle times in the schedule, it does help the scheduler to decide which frequency would best result in more reduction of power consumption. Especially, as we discussed previously, when there are some tasks which have to be scheduled using their original periods, the extra time scheduled for the tasks using pinwheel model can be further used for more reduction of power consumption.

div.head: Applying to POP-LG
div.p: Most of the power-aware scheduling algorithms use DVS and DFS of processor to reduce the power consumption, and the key idea is to exploit the system idle time. The system idle time is defined as the free time budgets currently in the system. For example, in [9], there are several power-aware scheduling algorithms using pinwheel model. However, the problem of tasks not allowing pinwheel transformation was not addressed. One of the proposed algorithm, called POP-LP, is based on the pinwheel model and use the linear programming technique to exploit the system idle time aggressively. At first, the pinwheel transformation using HSx [10] was applied on a given real-time task set. The HSx algorithm will find a best-effort pinwheel transformation and produce harmonic integer periods. The utilization bound of the transformed task set is still the same with the RM algorithm but the system predictability is increased. It will then become less time-consuming to determine the processor frequency of each real-time job. Usually, a real-time system schedules at necessary rescheduling points, such as when a task finishes its job, a high-priority task is ready for executing, etc. When the algorithm tries to determine the processor frequency for a real-time job at rescheduling points, especially when lowering frequencies, actually lengthening execution times, the algorithm will check on real-time jobs to make sure that no real-time task misses its timing constraints after this frequency change. The proposed algorithms find the next system idle time and they schedule within this interval (between two consecutive ends of idle times) at every rescheduling point. With the help of pinwheel algorithm, the number of real-time jobs we need to check is massively reduced due to the nature of harmonic periods. Hence, the number of rescheduling points is also massively reduced.

In the POP-LP algorithm, it reschedules at the next idle time for less power consumption. Since the next idle time can be found in polynomial time using pinwheel scheduling model, the pinwheel scheduling model can be applied efficiently in the power-aware real-time scheduling. However, if some tasks do not allow period transformation, from Theorem 1, there are still enough execution time scheduled in each original period. For this kind of tasks, we can set a budget counter for each task. If the task has used up its execution time, leave the system idle. We can also make use of these extra system idle time derived from pinwheel scheduling model to further reduce power consumption. Figure 8 shows the power-aware scheduling result making use of the extra idle time from the same task set in Figure 3. The darker bar is the low-power execution using the extra idle time.

div.head: Conclusion and Future Work
div.p: In this paper, we introduce rate monotonic scheduling algorithm in periodic task model and pinwheel scheduling algorithm in distance-constrained task model. While rate monotonic algorithm is optimal using priority-driven scheduling approach, pinwheel scheduling algorithm has high predictability and the schedule can be derived in polynomial time. If some tasks do not allow pinwheel transformation to shorten periods, we can still use pinwheel scheduling model to derive regular schedule with harmonic periods and use the original period to schedule these special tasks. It is proved that there is enough execution time in the original period. Therefore, pinwheel scheduling algorithm can also be applied in periodic task model. We show that the harmonic nature of pinwheel scheduling model can be easily applied to power-aware real-time scheduling and reduce computation time complexity. The extra idle time resulting from pinwheel scheduling model for the tasks do not allow period transformation can be used to further reduce power consumption.

Although it is complex to find the extra idle time in general, it is still tractable and much more efficient than other existing approaches. Our future work will focus on adding special hardware assistance such as special timers to reduce the time complexity to deal with the extra idle time. If we do not want to make use of the extra idle time, pinwheel scheduling model can be applied generally in periodic task model with the same schedulability bound of rate monotonic algorithm.
